Reference: Bombardini et al. (2025)

Model Setting

The paper asks how climate change and the employment changes that come with mitigation affect electoral politics in the United States, and whether democratic competition will deliver more climate policy as the climate deteriorates. It first estimates voter demand: using a 2000-2020 panel of precinct-level returns for the House of Representatives assigned to census block-groups, it regresses the Democratic vote margin on extreme temperature and precipitation days and on the local shares of green jobs and brown jobs, with congressional district-by-election fixed effects that hold candidates and platforms fixed. It then estimates policy supply: the environmental platforms of Democratic and Republican candidates are modelled as linear functions of the same shocks, of the expected vote margin and of a party-specific shifter, and the three-equation system is estimated by GMM. The structure is deliberately linear. It is not a discrete-choice demand system with random coefficients: there is no abstention margin, no inversion of market shares and no micro-moments, and voters' policy preferences enter only through the coefficients on the two platforms. A probabilistic voting model in the appendix provides the microfoundation. The reduced form of the system is finally iterated forward from 2022 to 2050 under climate and employment projections.

The main findings are as follows. A one standard deviation increase in extreme heat days raises the Democratic margin by about 0.7 percentage points and a one standard deviation increase in the brown job share lowers it by 0.62 percentage points, so weather and employment shocks have comparable effects on demand. Democratic candidates respond strongly to expected vote margins (a safer seat lets them move left), Republican candidates respond weakly and in the opposite direction, and voters respond to the Democratic platform but hardly to the Republican one. Local party delegations pass through to platforms at a rate of about 0.2, far below one. In the projections under the worst-case climate scenario the average Democratic margin rises by 1.4 percentage points by 2050 because of temperature, both parties move slightly to the right on the environment, Democrats gain four seats, and the probability that the House passes a carbon-pricing bill is 9 percentage points higher in 2050 than in 2020.

Data

Voting data are precinct-level returns from Longuet-Marx (2024). A precinct has on average 1,200 registered voters, about 60 times fewer than a county and 400 times fewer than a congressional district. Because precinct boundaries change, votes are assigned to 2010 census block-groups, which gives a stable panel of 1,339,268 block-group-by-election observations in the baseline regressions. Weather comes from an updated version of the Schlenker and Roberts (2009) daily grid (2.5 by 2.5 mile cells). For each grid cell and calendar day the mean and standard deviation of average daily temperature and of precipitation are computed over 1959-1999, and a day from 2000 onward is extreme if it exceeds the historical mean for that calendar day by two historical standard deviations. The regressors are the yearly counts of such days, interpolated to census blocks from the four nearest grid cells with inverse-distance weights and aggregated with population weights. Candidate positions on the environment are the campaign platforms of Longuet-Marx (2024): a Bayesian item response model is fitted to the environment questions of the Project Vote Smart candidate survey, and the scores are then predicted for all candidates, winners and losers, from the text of their campaign websites archived by the Library of Congress. Higher values are more conservative. For winners the platforms have a correlation of 0.866 with environment-specific roll-call ideal points (0.417 among Democrats and 0.333 among Republicans). Climate projections are from the NASA NEX-GDDP dataset (CESM2 model, 25 kilometre grid) under the scenarios SSP1-2.6 (optimistic, warming below 2 degrees Celsius) and SSP5-8.5 (emissions continue on historical trends), and employment projections are from the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook for 2023-2033, extended to 2050.

Measuring Green and Brown Employment

Green industries are the six-digit NAICS industries of the 2011 BLS Green Goods and Services survey, which also gives the share of each industry's employment devoted to green activities. Brown industries are eight six-digit industries in oil and gas extraction, coal mining and their support activities, all inside NAICS sector 21. Employment of the residents of block-group bbb is observed only at the two-digit level, so green employment in six-digit industry iii is imputed from commuting flows and from the industry mix of the counties where residents work (year subscripts omitted):

Voter Demand Within Districts

The demand specification at the block-group level is:

ybt=δtempTempbt+δprecPrecipbt+δbrownShBrEmpbt+δgreenShGrEmpbt+αXbt+μb+Ωc(b),t+ϵbt(4)\begin{aligned} y_{bt}&=\delta^{temp}Temp_{bt}+\delta^{prec}Precip_{bt}+\delta^{brown}ShBrEmp_{bt}+\delta^{green}ShGrEmp_{bt}\\ &\quad+\alpha X_{bt}+\mu_b+\Omega_{c(b),t}+\epsilon_{bt} \end{aligned} \tag{4}ybt​​=δtempTempbt​+δprecPrecipbt​+δbrownShBrEmpbt​+δgreenShGrEmpbt​+αXbt​+μb​+Ωc(b),t​+ϵbt​​(4)

where ybty_{bt}ybt​ is the Democratic minus the Republican vote share in block-group bbb and election year ttt (in percentage points), TempbtTemp_{bt}Tempbt​ and PrecipbtPrecip_{bt}Precipbt​ are the counts of extreme days, XbtX_{bt}Xbt​ are time-varying demographic controls, μb\mu_bμb​ are block-group fixed effects and Ωc(b),t\Omega_{c(b),t}Ωc(b),t​ are fixed effects for the congressional race, that is for district c(b)c(b)c(b) (defined within a redistricting cycle) in year ttt. The race fixed effects absorb everything that varies only across races, in particular both candidates' platforms and valence. This is the central identification argument for demand: in canonical models of electoral competition platforms depend on expected voter behaviour, so demand parameters cannot be recovered without conditioning on platforms, and the granularity of the data makes it possible to condition on them non-parametrically. The remaining weather variation is still substantial; its share of total variance ranges from 3.4 percent in Illinois to 55.6 percent in Montana for temperature. Standard errors are clustered by race and by block-group.

In the baseline, the coefficient on extreme temperature days is 0.0822 (0.0224), on extreme precipitation days 0.0421 (0.0209), on the brown share −0.356-0.356−0.356 (0.0839) and on the green share 0.339 (0.112). A one standard deviation increase in extreme heat days (8.13 days) therefore raises the Democratic margin by about 0.67 percentage points, one standard deviation of extreme precipitation (6.74 days) by about 0.28, one standard deviation of the brown share lowers it by 0.62, and one standard deviation of the green share raises it by 0.21. The summed absolute effect of one standard deviation of the two climate shocks is 0.951 (0.220) and of the two job shocks 0.834 (0.158). Adding media-market-by-year fixed effects or Conley standard errors with radii of 25 to 100 kilometres changes little. Dropping the block-group fixed effects multiplies the temperature and precipitation coefficients by 5.6 and 3.4 and turns the green coefficient negative (−3.953-3.953−3.953), which the paper attributes to sorting and to violations of the stable unit treatment value assumption; the specification with block-group fixed effects is retained as a lower bound. With the shift-share instruments (first-stage F statistic of 47.3) the brown coefficient is −0.753-0.753−0.753 (0.600) and the green coefficient rises to 6.395 (2.154), consistent with attenuation from measurement error in green employment. Two further checks support the interpretation as demand for climate policy. In Texas, the same shocks have similar or larger effects on the vote for Railroad Commissioners, elected regulators of the oil and gas industry, and remain significant there after controlling for the House vote. And, as the voting model below predicts, the effects of all shocks are larger in races where the exogenous component of the gap between the two candidates' positions is larger.

Probabilistic Voting Microfoundation

The appendix derives the empirical system from a standard probabilistic voting model. Two candidates DDD and RRR compete in a district with a continuum of voters iii with density f(i)f(i)f(i). Voter iii has an ideal point θi\theta_iθi​ in a multi-dimensional policy space and quadratic utility from a platform x\mathbf{x}x:

ui(x)=−∥x−θi∥2(5)u_i(\mathbf{x})=-\|\mathbf{x}-\theta_i\|^2 \tag{5}ui​(x)=−∥x−θi​∥2(5)

Candidate DDD has a commonly known net valence advantage δˉ\bar{\delta}δˉ. Voter iii receives ui(xD)+δˉ+ϵiu_i(\mathbf{x}_D)+\bar{\delta}+\epsilon_iui​(xD​)+δˉ+ϵi​ from DDD and ui(xR)u_i(\mathbf{x}_R)ui​(xR​) from RRR, where ϵi\epsilon_iϵi​ is an idiosyncratic shock drawn from a uniform distribution with mean zero and density ϕi\phi_iϕi​. A high ϕi\phi_iϕi​ marks a swing voter. The probability that voter iii votes for DDD is:

pi(xD,xR)=Pr⁡(ϵi>ui(xR)−ui(xD)−δˉ)=12+ϕi[ui(xD)−ui(xR)+δˉ](6)p_i(\mathbf{x}_D,\mathbf{x}_R)=\Pr\left(\epsilon_i>u_i(\mathbf{x}_R)-u_i(\mathbf{x}_D)-\bar{\delta}\right)=\frac{1}{2}+\phi_i\left[u_i(\mathbf{x}_D)-u_i(\mathbf{x}_R)+\bar{\delta}\right] \tag{6}pi​(xD​,xR​)=Pr(ϵi​>ui​(xR​)−ui​(xD​)−δˉ)=21​+ϕi​[ui​(xD​)−ui​(xR​)+δˉ](6)

The vote share is one half, plus a valence advantage, plus a policy advantage that rewards the candidate whose platform is closer to the electoral centre of gravity. The model delivers three lessons for the empirics. First, if the shocks V\mathbf{V}V move θD\theta_DθD​, θR\theta_RθR​, θˉϕ\bar{\theta}^{\phi}θˉϕ and δˉ\bar{\delta}δˉ at once, the direct effect of the shocks on voters can only be recovered holding candidates fixed, which is what the race fixed effects do. Second, the direct effect of the shocks on candidates' ideal points can only be recovered controlling for voter demand θˉϕ\bar{\theta}^{\phi}θˉϕ. Third, with platforms held fixed the derivative of the policy advantage with respect to θˉϕ\bar{\theta}^{\phi}θˉϕ is 2ϕˉ(xD∗−xR∗)2\bar{\phi}\left(\mathbf{x}^*_D-\mathbf{x}^*_R\right)2ϕˉ​(xD∗​−xR∗​), so a shock that moves voters to the left raises the Democratic share by more when the two platforms are farther apart; this is the heterogeneity confirmed in the demand estimates. The observed platforms xJ\mathbf{x}_JxJ​ are not the ideal points θJ\theta_JθJ​, and the party shifters zJ\mathbf{z}_JzJ​ are assumed to operate only through θJ\theta_JθJ​. The paper stresses that this model is one possible microfoundation, and the estimated system is linear in parameters and not the nonlinear form implied by the distance function.

In the estimation two elements are added to this just-identified core, and both make the system over-identified: δ\deltaδ is estimated from within-race block-group variation, which is far more precise than district-level variation, and second-moment restrictions on the three structural errors are imposed.

Estimation

Estimation has two steps. The first is the block-group demand regression, which gives δ^\hat{\delta}δ^ and the estimated race fixed effects Ω^ct\hat{\Omega}_{ct}Ω^ct​. In the second step, district and year fixed effects are partialled out of Vˉct\bar{\mathbf{V}}_{ct}Vˉct​, zctdz^d_{ct}zctd​, zctrz^r_{ct}zctr​, xctdx^d_{ct}xctd​, xctrx^r_{ct}xctr​, yˉct\bar{y}_{ct}yˉ​ct​ and Ω^ct\hat{\Omega}_{ct}Ω^ct​ by the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem; residualized variables carry a tilde. With η~ctd=x~ctd−(λdVˉ~ct+βdyˉ~ct+πdz~ctd)\tilde{\eta}^d_{ct}=\tilde{x}^d_{ct}-(\lambda^d\tilde{\bar{\mathbf{V}}}_{ct}+\beta^d\tilde{\bar{y}}_{ct}+\pi^d\tilde{z}^d_{ct})η~​ctd​=x~ctd​−(λdVˉ~ct​+βdyˉ​~​ct​+πdz~ctd​), η~ctr\tilde{\eta}^r_{ct}η~​ctr​ defined analogously and ε~ct=Ω~ct−γdx~ctd−γrx~ctr\tilde{\varepsilon}_{ct}=\tilde{\Omega}_{ct}-\gamma^d\tilde{x}^d_{ct}-\gamma^r\tilde{x}^r_{ct}ε~ct​=Ω~ct​−γdx~ctd​−γrx~ctr​, the sample moment conditions of the two-step GMM estimator are:

η~ctd⋅[Vˉ~ct′,z~ctd,z~ctr]=0,η~ctr⋅[Vˉ~ct′,z~ctd,z~ctr]=0,ε~ct⋅[z~ctd,z~ctr]=0Cov(η~ctd,η~ctr)=0,Cov(ε~ct,η~ctr)=0,Cov(η~ctd,ε~ct)=0(27)\begin{aligned} \tilde{\eta}^d_{ct}\cdot\left[\tilde{\bar{\mathbf{V}}}'_{ct},\tilde{z}^d_{ct},\tilde{z}^r_{ct}\right]&=\mathbf{0},\qquad\tilde{\eta}^r_{ct}\cdot\left[\tilde{\bar{\mathbf{V}}}'_{ct},\tilde{z}^d_{ct},\tilde{z}^r_{ct}\right]=\mathbf{0},\qquad\tilde{\varepsilon}_{ct}\cdot\left[\tilde{z}^d_{ct},\tilde{z}^r_{ct}\right]=\mathbf{0}\\ \text{Cov}\left(\tilde{\eta}^d_{ct},\tilde{\eta}^r_{ct}\right)&=0,\qquad\text{Cov}\left(\tilde{\varepsilon}_{ct},\tilde{\eta}^r_{ct}\right)=0,\qquad\text{Cov}\left(\tilde{\eta}^d_{ct},\tilde{\varepsilon}_{ct}\right)=0 \end{aligned} \tag{27}η~​ctd​⋅[Vˉ~ct′​,z~ctd​,z~ctr​]Cov(η~​ctd​,η~​ctr​)​=0,η~​ctr​⋅[Vˉ~ct′​,z~ctd​,z~ctr​]=0,ε~ct​⋅[z~ctd​,z~ctr​]=0=0,Cov(ε~ct​,η~​ctr​)=0,Cov(η~​ctd​,ε~ct​)=0​(27)

The first line states that the supply errors are orthogonal to the shocks and to both shifters and that the race-level demand shock is orthogonal to both shifters. The second line states that the three structural errors are mutually uncorrelated. Because the outcome Ω^ct\hat{\Omega}_{ct}Ω^ct​ of the demand moments is itself estimated, each race is weighted by the inverse of the variance of its estimated fixed effect. Standard errors are clustered by congressional district with a degrees-of-freedom correction for the number of equations.

Structural Estimates

Positions are scaled so that higher values are more conservative, and the margin is in percentage points. Standard errors are in parentheses.

  • Democratic supply: βd=−0.0195\beta^d=-0.0195βd=−0.0195 (0.0123), so a one standard deviation increase in the expected margin moves the Democratic candidate 0.63 points to the left, almost two standard deviations of Democratic positions. The local party effect is πd=0.1837\pi^d=0.1837πd=0.1837 (0.0795). The temperature component of λd\lambda^dλd is 0.0020 (0.0011): one standard deviation of extreme heat moves Democrats 0.016 points to the right, about 5 percent of the standard deviation of their positions, net of the effect through demand. The green and brown components are −0.1100-0.1100−0.1100 (0.1083) and 0.0301 (0.0292), which correspond to 0.043 points to the left and 0.034 points to the right per standard deviation; the precipitation component is 0.0013 (0.0014).

  • Republican supply: βr=0.0035\beta^r=0.0035βr=0.0035 (0.0014), less than one fifth of the Democratic response in standardized terms and of the opposite sign in ideological terms: a larger Democratic margin makes the Republican more conservative. The paper reads this as candidates with slim chances signalling their true stance, or as a larger weight on policy than on winning. The local party effect is πr=0.1972\pi^r=0.1972πr=0.1972 (0.0602). The components of λr\lambda^rλr are small and insignificant: −0.0008-0.0008−0.0008 (0.0015) for temperature, 0.0007 (0.0021) for precipitation, 0.1144 (0.0999) for green jobs and −0.0089-0.0089−0.0089 (0.0241) for brown jobs.

  • District demand: γd=24.81\gamma^d=24.81γd=24.81 (12.98) and γr=−1.32\gamma^r=-1.32γr=−1.32 (1.06). A one standard deviation move to the right (toward the centre) by the Democrat raises the Democratic margin by 8.6 percentage points according to the table (9.2 according to the text), whereas the same move by the Republican lowers it by about 0.6 percentage points. The components of δ\deltaδ are 0.0828 (0.0245) for temperature, 0.0443 (0.0231) for precipitation, 0.2160 (0.1174) for green jobs and −0.3562-0.3562−0.3562 (0.0927) for brown jobs.

  • Robustness and placebo: adding district-level employment, income and voting-age population to all three equations leaves the estimates robust. Re-estimating the system with candidates' cultural positions in place of environmental positions shows that none of the shocks moves cultural positions and that cultural positions do not move demand, although the neighbouring-delegation instruments remain relevant.

Both πd\pi^dπd and πr\pi^rπr are significantly below one, so local party delegations shape platforms without determining them. The point estimates imply βdγd≈−0.48\beta^d\gamma^d\approx-0.48βdγd≈−0.48 and hence Ξ≈0.67\Xi\approx0.67Ξ≈0.67: the feedback from margins to Democratic platforms and back to margins dampens every shock by about one third.

Direct and Indirect Effects

In the reduced form for the margin, the coefficient on a shock splits into a direct demand effect Ξδ\Xi\deltaΞδ and an indirect effect through platforms Ξ(γdλd+γrλr)\Xi\left(\gamma^d\lambda^d+\gamma^r\lambda^r\right)Ξ(γdλd+γrλr). In the reduced form for a platform it splits into the direct effect λp\lambda^pλp and the indirect effect through the margin βpΞ(δ+γdλd+γrλr)\beta^p\Xi\left(\delta+\gamma^d\lambda^d+\gamma^r\lambda^r\right)βpΞ(δ+γdλd+γrλr).

  • Temperature: the direct effect on the margin is 0.056 (0.024) and the indirect effect 0.034 (0.020), for a total of 0.089 (0.024) per extreme day. Heat makes Democrats slightly more moderate, and because voters reward moderation by Democrats the indirect effect is of the same order as the direct one. In equilibrium the Democratic platform does not move (total 0.000): the direct rightward shift is offset by the leftward shift that the larger margin allows.

  • Precipitation: direct 0.030 (0.018), indirect 0.021 (0.022), total 0.051 (0.028).

  • Brown jobs: the direct effect is −0.239-0.239−0.239 (0.095), but Democrats respond with more conservative platforms, the indirect effect is 0.509 (0.446) and the total 0.270 (0.452) is positive and insignificant.

  • Green jobs: the direct effect is 0.145 (0.092), but Democrats move left because of green jobs, which costs them votes: the indirect effect is −1.933-1.933−1.933 (1.625) and the total is −1.788-1.788−1.788 (1.657). The total effect on the Democratic platform is −0.075-0.075−0.075 (0.063), since the lower equilibrium margin pulls the platform part of the way back to the right. The paper's reading is that Democratic candidates overestimate how extreme a position green transition employment affords them.

  • Republican platforms: all total effects are small and insignificant, for example −0.008-0.008−0.008 (0.024) for brown jobs and 0.108 (0.101) for green jobs.

Projections for 2022-2050

The counterfactual exercise is a forward simulation of the reduced form. Starting from the observed yˉct\bar{y}_{ct}yˉ​ct​, xctdx^d_{ct}xctd​ and xctrx^r_{ct}xctr​ of each district in 2022, every two years the shifters zctdz^d_{ct}zctd​ and zctrz^r_{ct}zctr​ are rebuilt as the averages of the lagged platforms in adjacent districts, the projected weather shocks and job shares are inserted, and the reduced-form equations give yˉc,t+2\bar{y}_{c,t+2}yˉ​c,t+2​, xc,t+2dx^d_{c,t+2}xc,t+2d​ and xc,t+2rx^r_{c,t+2}xc,t+2r​, which serve as initial conditions for the next cycle. District and year fixed effects are held at their 2020 values, so there is no redistricting and no unobserved shock. Confidence intervals come from 5,000 bootstrap rounds that draw the structural coefficients from a multivariate normal distribution with the clustered GMM covariance matrix and resample residuals. The parsimony of the linear system is what makes this forward solution feasible.

  • Temperature: under SSP5-8.5 the average Democratic margin in 2050 is 1.39 percentage points higher than in 2022 (95 percent interval 0.63 to 2.15), of which 0.89 is the direct demand effect, 0.48 the indirect effect through Democratic platforms and 0.02 the effect through Republican platforms. Under SSP1-2.6 the total is 0.79 (0.36 to 1.21).

  • Precipitation: the total is 0.20 under SSP5-8.5 and 0.26 under SSP1-2.6, neither significant.

  • Employment: the BLS projects only a modest rise in the green share and a modest decline in the brown share, so the effects are tiny. For green jobs the change in the total contribution is −0.025-0.025−0.025 (−0.068-0.068−0.068 to 0.019) and for brown jobs −0.009-0.009−0.009 (−0.062-0.062−0.062 to 0.044). Mitigation through job composition is therefore not a major source of political change over this horizon, although extending the 2023-2033 trend to 2050 may understate later changes.

  • Geography: every district moves toward the Democrats. The largest temperature shocks are in Oklahoma, Colorado, Texas and Arizona, where extreme days rise by 68 on average under SSP5-8.5 and the Democratic margin rises by roughly 3 percentage points; Massachusetts, Illinois and Rhode Island gain less than 1 point. In the South platforms converge: Republicans become somewhat more progressive and Democrats more conservative. Democrats win four more seats in 2050 than in 2022, two of them in the South.

  • The House: the mean and median platforms of elected Democrats and of elected Republicans both become more conservative, yet the median member of the House becomes more liberal because the Democratic seat share rises. Mapping platforms into roll-call ideal points and using the 2009 Waxman-Markey cap-and-trade bill as the benchmark, the median member moves 0.11 units in the progressive direction and the probability of a yes vote on emissions pricing rises from 63 to 72 percent, that is by 9 percentage points.

The paper's conclusion is that weak voter demand does not explain limited climate action: demand responds to both weather and jobs. The response of supply is what limits policy change, since candidates do not move left as the climate worsens, and the projected gains come from the composition of the House and not from the platforms of either party.

This is an imputation formula, not an accounting identity. The data never show how many residents of block-group bbb work in the six-digit industry iii, so the number is built as a chain of observed objects under proportionality assumptions. Reading the summand from left to right:

Empb,k(i)⏟residents of b in sector k(i)×Empbc,l(i)Empb,l(i)⏟share commuting to c×EmpciEmpc,k(i)⏟share of i in sector k(i) of c×γj(i)⏟green share\underbrace{Emp_{b,k(i)}}_{\text{residents of } b \text{ in sector } k(i)}\times\underbrace{\frac{Emp_{bc,l(i)}}{Emp_{b,l(i)}}}_{\text{share commuting to } c}\times\underbrace{\frac{Emp_{ci}}{Emp_{c,k(i)}}}_{\text{share of } i \text{ in sector } k(i) \text{ of } c}\times\underbrace{\gamma_{j(i)}}_{\text{green share}}residents of b in sector k(i)Empb,k(i)​​​×share commuting to cEmpb,l(i)​Empbc,l(i)​​​​×share of i in sector k(i) of cEmpc,k(i)​Empci​​​​×green shareγj(i)​​​

The first two factors give the imputed number of residents of bbb who work in county ccc in sector k(i)k(i)k(i). The third factor splits them across six-digit industries with the industry mix of the workplace county. The fourth keeps only the green part of those jobs. Summing over the workplace counties c∈C(b)c\in C(b)c∈C(b) gives the green employment of residents of bbb in industry iii, measured in workers.

Three assumptions are implicit. First, the commuting pattern, observed only for the coarser supersector l(i)l(i)l(i), applies to every two-digit sector inside it. Second, residents of bbb who work in county ccc in sector k(i)k(i)k(i) are spread over six-digit industries like all workers of that county and sector. Third, the green share γj(i)\gamma_{j(i)}γj(i)​, measured for a four-digit industry, is common to all its six-digit industries and to all places. A consistency check: replace γj(i)\gamma_{j(i)}γj(i)​ by one and sum over all industries iii of a sector; the third factor then sums to one, the commuting shares sum to one over ccc, and the total is Empb,k(i)Emp_{b,k(i)}Empb,k(i)​. The imputation therefore only reallocates observed sector employment.

A numerical illustration: 200 residents in the sector, 60 percent of them commuting to county ccc, industry iii making up 10 percent of that sector in ccc, and γj(i)=0.5\gamma_{j(i)}=0.5γj(i)​=0.5 give 200×0.6×0.1×0.5=6200\times0.6\times0.1\times0.5=6200×0.6×0.1×0.5=6 green jobs from county ccc. The measurement error created by the three assumptions is why the shares are instrumented with equation (2), and why the rise of the green coefficient under IV is read as attenuation.

The left side is the predicted green employment of block-group bbb in year ttt per worker of 2000. Multiplying both sides by Empb,2000Emp_{b,2000}Empb,2000​ shows the logic:

GreenEmp^bt=∑i∈GGreenEmpbi,2000×GreenEmpitGreenEmpi,2000\widehat{GreenEmp}_{bt}=\sum_{i\in G}GreenEmp_{bi,2000}\times\frac{GreenEmp_{it}}{GreenEmp_{i,2000}}GreenEmp​bt​=i∈G∑​GreenEmpbi,2000​×GreenEmpi,2000​GreenEmpit​​

Each initial stock of green jobs, obtained from equation (1) in 2000, is grown at the national growth factor of its industry. In shift-share language the exposure shares are sbi=GreenEmpbi,2000/Empb,2000s_{bi}=GreenEmp_{bi,2000}/Emp_{b,2000}sbi​=GreenEmpbi,2000​/Empb,2000​ and the shifts are git=GreenEmpit/GreenEmpi,2000g_{it}=GreenEmp_{it}/GreenEmp_{i,2000}git​=GreenEmpit​/GreenEmpi,2000​. Nothing that happens locally after 2000 enters the prediction, so local changes in green employment that are themselves caused by local politics, or by the sorting of green-minded workers, are removed; what is left is the part of the change in the green share that comes from national industry trends hitting places with different initial industry mixes.

The shares do not sum to one:

∑i∈Gsbi=GreenEmpb,2000Empb,2000\sum_{i\in G}s_{bi}=\frac{GreenEmp_{b,2000}}{Emp_{b,2000}}i∈G∑​sbi​=Empb,2000​GreenEmpb,2000​​

which is the green share of 2000. In the special case of a common shift git=gtg_{it}=g_tgit​=gt​ the instrument equals gtg_tgt​ times this initial share, so it would vary across places only through initial greenness, which may be correlated with political leanings. This is the incomplete-shares problem of Borusyak, Hull and Jaravel (2022): the sum of shares must be controlled for so that identification comes from the shifts. Block-group fixed effects μb\mu_bμb​ absorb the time-invariant sum; without them it is added as a control. The brown instrument is built in the same way with the set BBB. In the note the first-stage F statistic is 47.3 and the IV coefficients are 6.395 for the green share and −0.753-0.753−0.753 for the brown share in equation (4).

This is the estimating equation for voter demand. The outcome ybty_{bt}ybt​ is the Democratic minus the Republican vote share in percentage points. TempbtTemp_{bt}Tempbt​ and PrecipbtPrecip_{bt}Precipbt​ are counts of extreme days, so δtemp\delta^{temp}δtemp and δprec\delta^{prec}δprec are percentage points of margin per extreme day; the shares ShBrEmpbtShBrEmp_{bt}ShBrEmpbt​ and ShGrEmpbtShGrEmp_{bt}ShGrEmpbt​ are in percentage points, so δbrown\delta^{brown}δbrown and δgreen\delta^{green}δgreen are points of margin per point of employment share. μb\mu_bμb​ removes everything permanent about a block-group (partisanship, geography, average climate), and the race fixed effect Ωc(b),t\Omega_{c(b),t}Ωc(b),t​ removes everything common to voters who face the same pair of candidates: both platforms, both valences, national and district swings.

The identifying variation is therefore the deviation of a block-group from its own mean and from the mean of its race in that year: within one race, do the block-groups hit by more extreme days, or by a larger change in job shares, vote more Democratic than usual? Because platforms respond to expected votes, equations (15) and (18), they are endogenous to demand; holding them fixed non-parametrically through Ωc(b),t\Omega_{c(b),t}Ωc(b),t​ is what makes the coefficients demand parameters. The estimated Ω^ct\hat{\Omega}_{ct}Ω^ct​ are reused as the outcome of equation (17).

Voter iii has an ideal point θi\theta_iθi​, a vector with one entry per policy dimension, and loses utility in proportion to the squared Euclidean distance between the platform and that ideal point:

ui(x)=−∑j(xj−θij)2u_i(\mathbf{x})=-\sum_j\left(x_j-\theta_{ij}\right)^2ui​(x)=−j∑​(xj​−θij​)2

Utility is at most zero and is reached only at x=θi\mathbf{x}=\theta_ix=θi​. The quadratic form buys three things. First, the loss is additively separable across dimensions, so the first-order condition for the environmental dimension kkk involves only xkx_kxk​ and θik\theta_{ik}θik​; this is why the note can treat one dimension at a time in equations (9) and (11). Second, marginal utility is linear in the platform,

∂ui(x)∂xk=−2(xk−θik)\frac{\partial u_i(\mathbf{x})}{\partial x_k}=-2\left(x_k-\theta_{ik}\right)∂xk​∂ui​(x)​=−2(xk​−θik​)

so that, combined with the uniform shock of equation (6), the marginal vote share is linear and aggregation over voters depends only on a weighted mean of ideal points, equation (10). Third, strict concavity makes each candidate's problem strictly concave, so the first-order conditions are sufficient and the equilibrium platforms of equation (12) are unique.

What the form rules out: asymmetric losses (moving one unit left or right of the ideal point costs the same), different weights on different dimensions, and interactions between dimensions. All voters have the same curvature; heterogeneity enters only through θi\theta_iθi​ and through the responsiveness ϕi\phi_iϕi​. The difference of two quadratic losses is what later produces the nonlinear policy advantage in equations (13) and (14), which the empirical system replaces by the linear terms γdxctd+γrxctr\gamma^dx^d_{ct}+\gamma^rx^r_{ct}γdxctd​+γrxctr​ of equation (17).

Voter iii votes for DDD when the utility from DDD exceeds the utility from RRR:

ui(xD)+δˉ+ϵi>ui(xR)⟺ϵi>ai,ai=ui(xR)−ui(xD)−δˉu_i(\mathbf{x}_D)+\bar{\delta}+\epsilon_i>u_i(\mathbf{x}_R)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\epsilon_i>a_i,\qquad a_i=u_i(\mathbf{x}_R)-u_i(\mathbf{x}_D)-\bar{\delta}ui​(xD​)+δˉ+ϵi​>ui​(xR​)⟺ϵi​>ai​,ai​=ui​(xR​)−ui​(xD​)−δˉ

This is the first equality. For the second, a uniform distribution with mean zero and constant density ϕi\phi_iϕi​ must have a support of length 1/ϕi1/\phi_i1/ϕi​ centred at zero, that is the interval from −1/(2ϕi)-1/(2\phi_i)−1/(2ϕi​) to 1/(2ϕi)1/(2\phi_i)1/(2ϕi​). For a threshold aia_iai​ inside this interval, the probability of a draw above aia_iai​ is the density times the length of the interval to the right of aia_iai​:

Pr⁡(ϵi>ai)=ϕi(12ϕi−ai)=12−ϕiai=12+ϕi[ui(xD)−ui(xR)+δˉ]\begin{aligned} \Pr\left(\epsilon_i>a_i\right)&=\phi_i\left(\frac{1}{2\phi_i}-a_i\right)\\ &=\frac{1}{2}-\phi_ia_i\\ &=\frac{1}{2}+\phi_i\left[u_i(\mathbf{x}_D)-u_i(\mathbf{x}_R)+\bar{\delta}\right] \end{aligned}Pr(ϵi​>ai​)​=ϕi​(2ϕi​1​−ai​)=21​−ϕi​ai​=21​+ϕi​[ui​(xD​)−ui​(xR​)+δˉ]​

which is the equation in the note. A voter who is indifferent on policy and valence votes for DDD with probability one half; every unit of utility advantage of DDD raises the probability by ϕi\phi_iϕi​. A high ϕi\phi_iϕi​ means a narrow support of the shock, hence a voter whose choice is easily moved by policy: a swing voter.

An assumption is left unstated in the note and in the paper: the formula holds only for an interior threshold,

∣ui(xD)−ui(xR)+δˉ∣≤12ϕi\left|u_i(\mathbf{x}_D)-u_i(\mathbf{x}_R)+\bar{\delta}\right|\leq\frac{1}{2\phi_i}​ui​(xD​)−ui​(xR​)+δˉ​≤2ϕi​1​

Otherwise the probability is zero or one and the linearity that drives equations (11) to (14) fails. The standard treatment assumes that the support is wide enough for all voters at all relevant platforms.

The expected vote share of DDD is the population average of the individual probabilities of equation (6), with f(i)f(i)f(i) the density of voters, so that ∫f(i) di=1\int f(i)\,di=1∫f(i)di=1. With a continuum of voters and independent shocks the realized share equals the expected share, so candidates face no aggregate uncertainty about shares. Because nobody abstains, ΠR=1−ΠD\Pi_R=1-\Pi_DΠR​=1−ΠD​ and the vote margin is ΠD−ΠR=2ΠD−1\Pi_D-\Pi_R=2\Pi_D-1ΠD​−ΠR​=2ΠD​−1, which is used in equation (14).

Substituting equation (6) shows the structure that the rest of the model exploits:

ΠD=12+δˉ∫ϕif(i) di+∫ϕiui(xD)f(i) di−∫ϕiui(xR)f(i) di\Pi_D=\frac{1}{2}+\bar{\delta}\int\phi_if(i)\,di+\int\phi_iu_i(\mathbf{x}_D)f(i)\,di-\int\phi_iu_i(\mathbf{x}_R)f(i)\,diΠD​=21​+δˉ∫ϕi​f(i)di+∫ϕi​ui​(xD​)f(i)di−∫ϕi​ui​(xR​)f(i)di

The share is one half, plus a valence term, plus a term that depends only on the platform of DDD, minus a term that depends only on the platform of RRR. Two features matter. First, voters are weighted by their responsiveness ϕi\phi_iϕi​, not equally: swing voters count more, which is why the relevant centre of the electorate is the ϕ\phiϕ-weighted mean of equation (10) and not the median or the simple mean. Second, the share is additively separable in xD\mathbf{x}_DxD​ and xR\mathbf{x}_RxR​. The marginal effect of the platform of DDD on its vote share therefore does not depend on what RRR does, equation (11), which is the source of the dominant strategies behind equation (12).

In the empirical system the counterpart of 2ΠD−12\Pi_D-12ΠD​−1 is the district margin yˉct\bar{y}_{ct}yˉ​ct​ of equation (18), measured in percentage points.

Each candidate maximizes a weighted sum of two motives. The office motive is the expected vote share, ΠD\Pi_DΠD​ for DDD and 1−ΠD1-\Pi_D1−ΠD​ for RRR (there is no abstention). The policy motive is the quadratic loss from announcing a platform away from the candidate's own ideal point θJ=θ~J+ζJzJ\theta_J=\tilde{\theta}_J+\zeta_J\mathbf{z}_JθJ​=θ~J​+ζJ​zJ​, which combines a personal component and the preference of the local party delegation. The weight λJ∈[0,1]\lambda_J\in[0,1]λJ​∈[0,1] measures how much the candidate cares about policy relative to votes.

Two limiting cases fix ideas. With λJ=0\lambda_J=0λJ​=0 the candidate is purely office-seeking and, by equation (12), locates at the electoral centre θˉϕ\bar{\theta}^{\phi}θˉϕ: both candidates converge. With λJ=1\lambda_J=1λJ​=1 the candidate announces the own ideal point θJ\theta_JθJ​ whatever voters want. For interior λJ\lambda_JλJ​ the platform is a compromise, and the platforms of the two parties differ whenever their ideal points differ.

Several modelling choices should be noted. The office motive is linear in the vote share and not in the probability of winning, so a candidate values an extra vote equally in a safe and in a contested district; together with the uniform shock of equation (6) this removes any response of platforms to the expected margin, which is exactly the channel that the empirical parameters βd\beta^dβd and βr\beta^rβr of equation (15) add back. The policy loss depends on the candidate's own announced platform, not on the policy implemented by the winner, so the opponent's platform enters VJV_JVJ​ only through the vote share. The party shifter zJ\mathbf{z}_JzJ​ enters only through θJ\theta_JθJ​; this is the model counterpart of the exclusion restriction on zctdz^d_{ct}zctd​ and zctrz^r_{ct}zctr​, and ζJ\zeta_JζJ​ is the counterpart of the local party effects πd\pi^dπd and πr\pi^rπr.

These two definitions summarize the whole distribution of voters by two numbers per policy dimension. The first, ϕˉ\bar{\phi}ϕˉ​, is the population mean of the densities ϕi\phi_iϕi​: the average increase in the probability of voting for a candidate per unit of utility advantage, equation (6). It measures how responsive the electorate as a whole is to policy and to valence. The second, θˉkϕ\bar{\theta}^{\phi}_kθˉkϕ​, is a weighted mean of voters' ideal points on dimension kkk in which voter iii has weight ϕif(i)/ϕˉ\phi_if(i)/\bar{\phi}ϕi​f(i)/ϕˉ​; the weights are non-negative and integrate to one. Stacking the dimensions gives the vector θˉϕ\bar{\theta}^{\phi}θˉϕ, the electoral centre.

The weighting is the economic content. Voters with a high ϕi\phi_iϕi​ are swing voters whose choice reacts strongly to platforms, so candidates who chase votes cater to them; voters whose choice is dominated by the idiosyncratic shock (low ϕi\phi_iϕi​) carry little weight even if they are numerous. A two-group illustration: half the voters have ideal point 0 and responsiveness 3, the other half have ideal point 1 and responsiveness 1; then ϕˉ=2\bar{\phi}=2ϕˉ​=2 and θˉkϕ=(0.5×1×1)/2=0.25\bar{\theta}^{\phi}_k=(0.5\times1\times1)/2=0.25θˉkϕ​=(0.5×1×1)/2=0.25, well to the left of the unweighted mean 0.5.

These objects are sufficient statistics because the marginal vote share is linear, equation (11): platforms in equation (12) and vote shares in equations (13) and (14) depend on the electorate only through ϕˉ\bar{\phi}ϕˉ​ and θˉϕ\bar{\theta}^{\phi}θˉϕ. In the empirical reading, the shocks V\mathbf{V}V (weather, jobs) shift θˉϕ\bar{\theta}^{\phi}θˉϕ, which is what the demand coefficients δ\deltaδ of equations (4) and (16) capture.

The whole distribution of ideal points collapses to the single point θˉϕ\bar{\theta}^{\phi}θˉϕ: the dispersion of voters around it cancels between the two candidates. DDD gains votes when its platform is closer to the electoral centre than the platform of RRR. Nothing in these steps uses optimality, so the formula holds for any pair of platforms, not only the equilibrium one; this matters for the comparative statics with platforms held fixed that the note uses after equation (14).

The one half cancels: with equal valence and equally distant platforms the margin is zero. Here y∗y^*y∗ is a fraction between −1-1−1 and 1, whereas the empirical ybty_{bt}ybt​ is in percentage points.

The heterogeneity prediction quoted in the note (also the author's own derivation) follows by differentiating the policy advantage of the vote share, equation (13), with respect to the electoral centre, holding the platforms and ϕˉ\bar{\phi}ϕˉ​ fixed. Since the gradient of ∥x−θˉϕ∥2\|\mathbf{x}-\bar{\theta}^{\phi}\|^2∥x−θˉϕ∥2 with respect to θˉϕ\bar{\theta}^{\phi}θˉϕ is −2(x−θˉϕ)-2(\mathbf{x}-\bar{\theta}^{\phi})−2(x−θˉϕ),

which confirms the expression in the note. For the margin the derivative is twice as large, ∂y∗/∂θˉϕ=4ϕˉ(xD∗−xR∗)\partial y^*/\partial\bar{\theta}^{\phi}=4\bar{\phi}(\mathbf{x}^*_D-\mathbf{x}^*_R)∂y∗/∂θˉϕ=4ϕˉ​(xD∗​−xR∗​). Higher values are more conservative, so on the environmental dimension xDk∗<xRk∗x^*_{Dk}<x^*_{Rk}xDk∗​<xRk∗​ and the derivative is negative: a shock that lowers θˉkϕ\bar{\theta}^{\phi}_kθˉkϕ​ by a small amount Δ\DeltaΔ (voters move left) raises the Democratic share by 2ϕˉ(xRk∗−xDk∗)Δ2\bar{\phi}(x^*_{Rk}-x^*_{Dk})\Delta2ϕˉ​(xRk∗​−xDk∗​)Δ, an effect proportional to the distance between the two platforms and equal to zero if they coincide. This is the interaction tested in the demand estimates. In equilibrium the platforms also move with θˉϕ\bar{\theta}^{\phi}θˉϕ through equation (12), so this is the effect with candidates held fixed, the one isolated by the race fixed effects of equation (4).

These are the two policy supply equations, one per party p∈{d,r}p\in\{d,r\}p∈{d,r}. The outcome xctpx^p_{ct}xctp​ is the environmental platform of the party's candidate in district ccc and year ttt, on a scale where higher is more conservative. There are four ingredients. λpVˉct\lambda^p\bar{\mathbf{V}}_{ct}λpVˉct​: the direct effect of district weather and job conditions on the candidate's position, holding the margin fixed, to be read as a shift in the candidate's ideal point. βpyˉct\beta^p\bar{y}_{ct}βpyˉ​ct​: the response to the expected Democratic margin, with yˉct\bar{y}_{ct}yˉ​ct​ in percentage points; βd<0\beta^d<0βd<0 means that a safer Democrat moves left. πpzctp\pi^pz^p_{ct}πpzctp​: the pull of the local party, where the shifter is the mean platform of same-party candidates in adjacent districts of the state. Finally district effects ωcp\omega^p_cωcp​, year effects ζtp\zeta^p_tζtp​ and the error ηctp\eta^p_{ct}ηctp​, so identification uses changes within a district over time relative to the national trend of the party.

Compared with the microfoundation, equation (12), λp\lambda^pλp and πp\pi^pπp correspond to the weights on the candidate's ideal point and on zJ\mathbf{z}_JzJ​; the term in yˉct\bar{y}_{ct}yˉ​ct​ has no counterpart there, because platforms in that model are dominant strategies, and is an empirical generalization.

Two exclusion restrictions are built in and carry the identification of equations (22) to (26). The opponent's platform and the opponent's shifter do not enter: zctrz^r_{ct}zctr​ moves xctdx^d_{ct}xctd​ only through yˉct\bar{y}_{ct}yˉ​ct​, which identifies βd\beta^dβd, and symmetrically for βr\beta^rβr. And yˉct\bar{y}_{ct}yˉ​ct​ is endogenous, since by equation (18) it depends on both platforms, so the equations cannot be estimated by least squares. With the estimates of the note, a one standard deviation rise in the margin (about 32 percentage points across districts) moves the Democrat by −0.0195×32≈−0.63-0.0195\times32\approx-0.63−0.0195×32≈−0.63 and the Republican by 0.0035×32≈0.110.0035\times32\approx0.110.0035×32≈0.11.

This restates the block-group demand equation (4) in compact form: Vbt\mathbf{V}_{bt}Vbt​ stacks the two weather counts, the two job shares and the other covariates (the controls XbtX_{bt}Xbt​ of equation (4) are now part of it), and δ\deltaδ is the corresponding row vector of coefficients, so δVbt\delta\mathbf{V}_{bt}δVbt​ is a scalar in percentage points of margin. Ωct\Omega_{ct}Ωct​ is the race fixed effect of the district c=c(b)c=c(b)c=c(b) in which the block-group lies, μb\mu_bμb​ the block-group fixed effect and εbt\varepsilon_{bt}εbt​ the error (written ϵbt\epsilon_{bt}ϵbt​ in equation (4); the two notations are the paper's).

The equation plays two roles in the system. First, it delivers δ^\hat{\delta}δ^ from within-race variation across more than a million block-group observations, which is far more precise than anything district-level data could give; in the logic of the voting model, δ\deltaδ measures how the shocks move the electoral centre θˉϕ\bar{\theta}^{\phi}θˉϕ with candidates held fixed. Second, it delivers the estimated race effects Ω^ct\hat{\Omega}_{ct}Ω^ct​, the part of the vote common to a race after removing local shocks and permanent block-group differences. These become the dependent variable of equation (17), where they are explained by the two platforms. Averaging the equation over the block-groups of a district gives the district demand function, equation (18).

A caveat on the numbers: the paper states that the demand effects in the structural table are by construction those of the block-group regression, and for temperature, precipitation and brown jobs they are (0.0828, 0.0443 and −0.3562-0.3562−0.3562 against 0.0822, 0.0421 and −0.356-0.356−0.356). For green jobs the structural table reports 0.2160 while the block-group table reports 0.339. The paper does not explain the gap, and the note reports each number in its own place.

In the first step the race fixed effect Ωct\Omega_{ct}Ωct​ is left unrestricted. This equation gives it structure: the common component of the vote in a race is a linear function of the two platforms, a district effect μc\mu_cμc​, a year effect κt\kappa_tκt​ and a race-level shock εct\varepsilon_{ct}εct​. Since higher platforms are more conservative and the outcome is the Democratic margin, γd>0\gamma^d>0γd>0 means that voters reward a Democrat who moves toward the centre, and γr<0\gamma^r<0γr<0 means that the Democratic margin falls when the Republican moves further right. The shock εct\varepsilon_{ct}εct​ collects everything else about the race, such as candidate quality, scandals and campaign spending; it is the counterpart of the valence δˉ\bar{\delta}δˉ of the voting model.

The equation is the linear stand-in for the policy advantage of equation (14). There the margin depends on the difference of two squared distances, so the marginal effect of a platform depends on its distance from the electoral centre; here it is a constant. A first-order expansion of equation (14) around given platforms gives

∂y∗∂xDk=−4ϕˉ(xDk−θˉkϕ),∂y∗∂xRk=4ϕˉ(xRk−θˉkϕ)\frac{\partial y^*}{\partial x_{Dk}}=-4\bar{\phi}\left(x_{Dk}-\bar{\theta}^{\phi}_k\right),\qquad\frac{\partial y^*}{\partial x_{Rk}}=4\bar{\phi}\left(x_{Rk}-\bar{\theta}^{\phi}_k\right)∂xDk​∂y∗​=−4ϕˉ​(xDk​−θˉkϕ​),∂xRk​∂y∗​=4ϕˉ​(xRk​−θˉkϕ​)

With the Democrat to the left of the centre and the Republican to the right, the model predicts γd>0\gamma^d>0γd>0 and γr>0\gamma^r>0γr>0. The estimates are γd=24.81\gamma^d=24.81γd=24.81 and γr=−1.32\gamma^r=-1.32γr=−1.32 (insignificant): the Democratic sign agrees with the model and the Republican one does not, which is one reason the paper calls the model only one possible microfoundation.

Platforms are endogenous in this equation because, by equation (15), they respond to the margin and hence to εct\varepsilon_{ct}εct​. The party shifters zctdz^d_{ct}zctd​ and zctrz^r_{ct}zctr​, excluded from demand, serve as instruments; see equation (24) and the third moment condition in equation (27).

Start from the block-group demand, equation (16), and substitute the parameterized race effect, equation (17):

ybt=δVbt+γdxctd+γrxctr+μc+κt+εct+μb+εbty_{bt}=\delta\mathbf{V}_{bt}+\gamma^dx^d_{ct}+\gamma^rx^r_{ct}+\mu_c+\kappa_t+\varepsilon_{ct}+\mu_b+\varepsilon_{bt}ybt​=δVbt​+γdxctd​+γrxctr​+μc​+κt​+εct​+μb​+εbt​

Let wbw_bwb​ be the population weight of block-group bbb in district ccc, with ∑b∈cwb=1\sum_{b\in c}w_b=1∑b∈c​wb​=1, and take the weighted average over the block-groups of the district. Terms that vary only by race, district or year are unchanged by averaging; the block-group terms become district averages:

yˉct=∑b∈cwbybt,Vˉct=∑b∈cwbVbt,μˉc=∑b∈cwbμb,εˉct=∑b∈cwbεbt\bar{y}_{ct}=\sum_{b\in c}w_by_{bt},\qquad\bar{\mathbf{V}}_{ct}=\sum_{b\in c}w_b\mathbf{V}_{bt},\qquad\bar{\mu}_c=\sum_{b\in c}w_b\mu_b,\qquad\bar{\varepsilon}_{ct}=\sum_{b\in c}w_b\varepsilon_{bt}yˉ​ct​=b∈c∑​wb​ybt​,Vˉct​=b∈c∑​wb​Vbt​,μˉ​c​=b∈c∑​wb​μb​,εˉct​=b∈c∑​wb​εbt​

Since δ\deltaδ is a constant vector, the average of δVbt\delta\mathbf{V}_{bt}δVbt​ is δVˉct\delta\bar{\mathbf{V}}_{ct}δVˉct​. Hence

yˉct=δVˉct+γdxctd+γrxctr+(μc+μˉc)+κt+(εct+εˉct)\bar{y}_{ct}=\delta\bar{\mathbf{V}}_{ct}+\gamma^dx^d_{ct}+\gamma^rx^r_{ct}+\left(\mu_c+\bar{\mu}_c\right)+\kappa_t+\left(\varepsilon_{ct}+\bar{\varepsilon}_{ct}\right)yˉ​ct​=δVˉct​+γdxctd​+γrxctr​+(μc​+μˉ​c​)+κt​+(εct​+εˉct​)

Collecting νc=μc+μˉc\nu_c=\mu_c+\bar{\mu}_cνc​=μc​+μˉ​c​ and ξct=εct+εˉct\xi_{ct}=\varepsilon_{ct}+\bar{\varepsilon}_{ct}ξct​=εct​+εˉct​ gives the equation of the note.

Two remarks. First, the linearity of equation (16) is what lets the same δ\deltaδ appear at both levels; no aggregation bias arises. Second, an assumption is implicit: μˉc\bar{\mu}_cμˉ​c​ carries no time index, which requires the set of block-groups of a district and their weights to be constant over time. This holds within a redistricting cycle if population weights are fixed, and districts are defined within a cycle; otherwise the term would vary with ttt and would not be absorbed by a district fixed effect. With many block-groups per district the average εˉct\bar{\varepsilon}_{ct}εˉct​ is small, so ξct\xi_{ct}ξct​ is essentially the race-level valence shock εct\varepsilon_{ct}εct​. Together with the two supply equations (15), this equation forms the three-equation system whose solution is the reduced form of equations (20) and (21).

These are the composite objects that appear when the three structural equations (15) and (18) are solved for the three endogenous variables; their origin is shown in the derivation of equation (20). αct\alpha_{ct}αct​ and ρctp\rho^p_{ct}ρctp​ merely collect the fixed effects of demand and of each supply equation. Λct\Lambda_{ct}Λct​ is the total shock to the margin before feedback: the demand shock ξct\xi_{ct}ξct​ plus the two supply shocks, each converted into margin units by the sensitivity of the margin to that platform.

The multiplier Ξ\XiΞ is the key object. An exogenous push of one point to the margin changes the two platforms by βd\beta^dβd and βr\beta^rβr, equation (15), which changes the margin again by βdγd+βrγr\beta^d\gamma^d+\beta^r\gamma^rβdγd+βrγr, equation (18), and so on. Summing the geometric series,

1+(βdγd+βrγr)+(βdγd+βrγr)2+⋯=11−βdγd−βrγr=Ξ1+\left(\beta^d\gamma^d+\beta^r\gamma^r\right)+\left(\beta^d\gamma^d+\beta^r\gamma^r\right)^2+\dots=\frac{1}{1-\beta^d\gamma^d-\beta^r\gamma^r}=\Xi1+(βdγd+βrγr)+(βdγd+βrγr)2+⋯=1−βdγd−βrγr1​=Ξ

which converges when ∣βdγd+βrγr∣<1|\beta^d\gamma^d+\beta^r\gamma^r|<1∣βdγd+βrγr∣<1; the system has a unique solution whenever βdγd+βrγr≠1\beta^d\gamma^d+\beta^r\gamma^r\neq1βdγd+βrγr=1. If the loop is negative, Ξ<1\Xi<1Ξ<1 and the feedback dampens shocks; if it is positive, shocks are amplified.

The value Ξ≈0.67\Xi\approx0.67Ξ≈0.67 in the note is the author's own computation from the point estimates, and it is correct:

βdγd=−0.0195×24.8117=−0.4838,βrγr=0.0035×(−1.3158)=−0.0046,Ξ=11+0.4838+0.0046=11.4884=0.672\begin{aligned} \beta^d\gamma^d&=-0.0195\times24.8117=-0.4838,\qquad\beta^r\gamma^r=0.0035\times(-1.3158)=-0.0046,\\ \Xi&=\frac{1}{1+0.4838+0.0046}=\frac{1}{1.4884}=0.672 \end{aligned}βdγdΞ​=−0.0195×24.8117=−0.4838,βrγr=0.0035×(−1.3158)=−0.0046,=1+0.4838+0.00461​=1.48841​=0.672​

A higher margin lets the Democrat move left, which costs votes, so about one third of any shock to the margin is undone. Almost all the feedback runs through the Democratic platform. The value is confirmed by the paper's own reduced-form table: the direct temperature effect there, 0.056, equals Ξδtemp=0.672×0.0828\Xi\delta^{temp}=0.672\times0.0828Ξδtemp=0.672×0.0828.

This is an indirect least squares (Wald) estimator: the opponent's shifter is the instrument for the margin in a party's supply equation, the denominator is the first stage and the numerator the reduced form. The multiplier cancels, so the feedback loop need not be known.

The ratios require non-zero denominators: ky,zr≠0k_{y,z^r}\neq0ky,zr​=0 needs γr≠0\gamma^r\neq0γr=0 and πr≠0\pi^r\neq0πr=0, and ky,zd≠0k_{y,z^d}\neq0ky,zd​=0 needs γd≠0\gamma^d\neq0γd=0 and πd≠0\pi^d\neq0πd=0. This relevance condition is not stated in the note. By contrast βr\beta^rβr is identified from the strong effect of the Democratic shifter on the margin (Ξγdπd≈3.06\Xi\gamma^d\pi^d\approx3.06Ξγdπd≈3.06).

which is the expression of the note; the leading minus sign only reflects the order in which the numerator is written. The logic is to subtract from the total response of a platform to its own shifter the part that is a reaction to the induced change in the margin, leaving the structural pass-through of the local party. Numerically, with the estimates of the note, the reduced-form own-shifter slopes are Ξπd(1−βrγr)=0.672×0.1837×1.0046=0.124\Xi\pi^d(1-\beta^r\gamma^r)=0.672\times0.1837\times1.0046=0.124Ξπd(1−βrγr)=0.672×0.1837×1.0046=0.124 and Ξπr(1−βdγd)=0.672×0.1972×1.4838=0.197\Xi\pi^r(1-\beta^d\gamma^d)=0.672\times0.1972\times1.4838=0.197Ξπr(1−βdγd)=0.672×0.1972×1.4838=0.197: for Democrats the structural effect 0.184 exceeds the reduced-form slope because a Democrat pulled to the right gains votes and then moves back left.

The district demand equation (18) holds for the equilibrium values of the margin and of the platforms, and the shifters zctdz^d_{ct}zctd​ and zctrz^r_{ct}zctr​ do not enter it directly. Taking the reduced-form slope of both sides with respect to each shifter (equivalently, projecting demand on the exogenous variables) gives two linear equations in γd\gamma^dγd and γr\gamma^rγr:

ky,zd=γdkxd,zd+γrkxr,zdky,zr=γdkxd,zr+γrkxr,zr\begin{aligned} k_{y,z^d}&=\gamma^dk_{x^d,z^d}+\gamma^rk_{x^r,z^d}\\ k_{y,z^r}&=\gamma^dk_{x^d,z^r}+\gamma^rk_{x^r,z^r} \end{aligned}ky,zd​ky,zr​​=γdkxd,zd​+γrkxr,zd​=γdkxd,zr​+γrkxr,zr​​

A shifter moves the margin only by moving the two platforms. Solve by Cramer's rule with determinant Δ=kxd,zdkxr,zr−kxd,zrkxr,zd\Delta=k_{x^d,z^d}k_{x^r,z^r}-k_{x^d,z^r}k_{x^r,z^d}Δ=kxd,zd​kxr,zr​−kxd,zr​kxr,zd​:

which are the formulas of the note. This is the just-identified instrumental-variables estimator of demand with two endogenous regressors (the platforms) and two instruments (the shifters): the matrix of slopes of platforms on shifters is the first stage and the slopes of the margin on shifters are the reduced form.

The two equations can be checked against the structural expressions. Using kxd,zd=Ξπd(1−βrγr)k_{x^d,z^d}=\Xi\pi^d(1-\beta^r\gamma^r)kxd,zd​=Ξπd(1−βrγr), kxr,zd=Ξπdβrγdk_{x^r,z^d}=\Xi\pi^d\beta^r\gamma^dkxr,zd​=Ξπdβrγd and ky,zd=Ξγdπdk_{y,z^d}=\Xi\gamma^d\pi^dky,zd​=Ξγdπd, the first equation reads Ξγdπd=Ξγdπd(1−βrγr)+Ξγrπdβrγd\Xi\gamma^d\pi^d=\Xi\gamma^d\pi^d(1-\beta^r\gamma^r)+\Xi\gamma^r\pi^d\beta^r\gamma^dΞγdπd=Ξγdπd(1−βrγr)+Ξγrπdβrγd, which holds. The rank condition is Δ≠0\Delta\neq0Δ=0, and the determinant has a simple form:

These hold component by component: λp\lambda^pλp, δ\deltaδ and the slopes on Vˉct\bar{\mathbf{V}}_{ct}Vˉct​ are vectors with one entry per shock, while βp\beta^pβp is a scalar. The economic content: the observed response of a platform to weather or jobs mixes a change in the candidate's own preferences with a reaction to the change in electoral prospects; subtracting the latter, priced at βp\beta^pβp, isolates the former. Temperature shows why this matters. In equilibrium the Democratic platform does not move with temperature (kxd,Vˉ≈0.000k_{x^d,\bar{\mathbf{V}}}\approx0.000kxd,Vˉ​≈0.000), while the margin rises by ky,Vˉ=0.089k_{y,\bar{\mathbf{V}}}=0.089ky,Vˉ​=0.089 per extreme day; hence λd=0.000−(−0.0195)(0.089)≈0.002\lambda^d=0.000-(-0.0195)(0.089)\approx0.002λd=0.000−(−0.0195)(0.089)≈0.002, a rightward direct effect hidden by the leftward move that the larger margin permits.

The reduced-form slope of the margin on the shocks, from equation (20), is

using the definition of Ξ\XiΞ in equation (19). Multiply both sides by 1−βdγd−βrγr1-\beta^d\gamma^d-\beta^r\gamma^r1−βdγd−βrγr and subtract the platform terms:

Every object on the right is already identified: βd\beta^dβd and βr\beta^rβr from equation (22), γd\gamma^dγd and γr\gamma^rγr from equation (24), λd\lambda^dλd and λr\lambda^rλr from equation (25). This completes the constructive argument: nine reduced-form slopes (three outcomes by three sets of exogenous variables) recover the nine structural parameters, with the recursive order β\betaβ, then π\piπ and λ\lambdaλ, then γ\gammaγ, then δ\deltaδ. The conditions needed along the way are βdγd+βrγr≠1\beta^d\gamma^d+\beta^r\gamma^r\neq1βdγd+βrγr=1 and non-zero γd\gamma^dγd, γr\gamma^rγr, πd\pi^dπd, πr\pi^rπr.

An equivalent reading: substituting λp=kxp,Vˉ−βpky,Vˉ\lambda^p=k_{x^p,\bar{\mathbf{V}}}-\beta^pk_{y,\bar{\mathbf{V}}}λp=kxp,Vˉ​−βpky,Vˉ​ from equation (25) simplifies the formula to

δ=ky,Vˉ−γdkxd,Vˉ−γrkxr,Vˉ\delta=k_{y,\bar{\mathbf{V}}}-\gamma^dk_{x^d,\bar{\mathbf{V}}}-\gamma^rk_{x^r,\bar{\mathbf{V}}}δ=ky,Vˉ​−γdkxd,Vˉ​−γrkxr,Vˉ​

so the direct demand effect is the total effect of the shock on the margin minus what is due to the induced equilibrium movements of the two platforms. A check with temperature: ky,Vˉ=0.0897k_{y,\bar{\mathbf{V}}}=0.0897ky,Vˉ​=0.0897 and equilibrium platform responses of 0.00030.00030.0003 and −0.0005-0.0005−0.0005 give 0.0897−24.81×0.0003−(−1.32)(−0.0005)≈0.0820.0897-24.81\times0.0003-(-1.32)(-0.0005)\approx0.0820.0897−24.81×0.0003−(−1.32)(−0.0005)≈0.082, close to δtemp=0.0828\delta^{temp}=0.0828δtemp=0.0828 (the gap is rounding of the tiny platform responses multiplied by the large γd\gamma^dγd).

In practice the paper does not estimate δ\deltaδ this way. It takes δ^\hat{\delta}δ^ from the block-group regression, equation (16), where platforms are held fixed by the race fixed effects; this uses within-race variation that the district-level formula cannot use, and it makes the system over-identified.

These are the moment conditions of the second step, written for variables from which district and year fixed effects have been partialled out (tildes). The residuals are the structural errors evaluated at trial parameter values: η~ctd\tilde{\eta}^d_{ct}η~​ctd​ and η~ctr\tilde{\eta}^r_{ct}η~​ctr​ from the supply equations (15), and ε~ct\tilde{\varepsilon}_{ct}ε~ct​ from equation (17) with the estimated Ω^ct\hat{\Omega}_{ct}Ω^ct​ as outcome. Each condition in the first line is shorthand for a sample average over races set to zero, for example

1N∑c,twct η~ctd z~ctr=0\frac{1}{N}\sum_{c,t}w_{ct}\,\tilde{\eta}^d_{ct}\,\tilde{z}^r_{ct}=0N1​c,t∑​wct​η~​ctd​z~ctr​=0

where NNN is the number of races and wctw_{ct}wct​ is the weight, the inverse of the sampling variance of Ω^ct\hat{\Omega}_{ct}Ω^ct​.

The first line contains the instrument-exogeneity conditions and reproduces the constructive argument of equations (22) to (25). In each supply equation the shocks Vˉ~ct\tilde{\bar{\mathbf{V}}}_{ct}Vˉ~ct​ and the own shifter are included regressors that serve as their own instruments, and the opponent's shifter is the excluded instrument for the endogenous margin yˉ~ct\tilde{\bar{y}}_{ct}yˉ​~​ct​; these conditions pin down λp\lambda^pλp, βp\beta^pβp and πp\pi^pπp exactly. In the demand equation the two shifters instrument the two platforms and pin down γd\gamma^dγd and γr\gamma^rγr. The shocks are not used as instruments for ε~ct\tilde{\varepsilon}_{ct}ε~ct​, and need not be: their effect δ\deltaδ was removed in the first step, and Ω^ct\hat{\Omega}_{ct}Ω^ct​ is by construction net of δ^Vbt\hat{\delta}\mathbf{V}_{bt}δ^Vbt​.

The second line adds three covariance restrictions: the two supply errors and the race-level demand shock are mutually uncorrelated. Economically, an unobserved reason for a Democrat to be unusually liberal is unrelated to the unobserved leaning of the opponent and to unobserved candidate valence. These are assumptions, not implications of the model, and they are the over-identifying restrictions. Counting with four shocks in Vˉct\bar{\mathbf{V}}_{ct}Vˉct​: the first line has 6+6+2=146+6+2=146+6+2=14 moments for the 14 parameters λd\lambda^dλd, λr\lambda^rλr (four each), βd\beta^dβd, βr\beta^rβr, πd\pi^dπd, πr\pi^rπr, γd\gamma^dγd, γr\gamma^rγr, so it is just-identified; the second line adds 3, giving 3 over-identifying restrictions. Two-step GMM then weights the 17 moments optimally. Since ε~ct\tilde{\varepsilon}_{ct}ε~ct​ does not contain δ\deltaδ, the demand coefficients are not re-estimated here, which makes the difference between the two reported green-job coefficients (0.2160 and 0.339) hard to reconcile.
